extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), judges, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for what a patent specification/description must contain and how it must be drafted so that a person skilled in the art can understand, make, and use the invention; covers correctness, completeness, intelligibility, enablement, claim certainty, and when ambiguity or concealment is fatal. Primarily U.S.-focused legal guidance with case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be correct
rubrics_metrics.description: A description is correct when the idea expressed by the words of which it consists corresponds exactly with the real nature of the thing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correctness requirement means the language must correspond with the actual invention and the acts to construct or use it. Whether a description is correct is a question of law (construction) and fact (truth of statements); the jury may decide factual issues. Slight errors in essentials or mistaken theories, wrong names, or erroneous classifications are tolerated so long as they do not mislead a cautious reader skilled in the art. However, statements that falsely purport essential operative features can be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be complete
rubrics_metrics.description: A description is complete when it embraces every essential part and attribute of the thing described; the specification is complete when, by following it precisely as it reads, a person skilled in the art could make and use the invention without addition or subtraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness requires disclosure of every essential part/attribute, but the law recognizes practical limitations: immaterial parts need not be detailed, familiar implements/processes need not be described, and omissions of minor details are acceptable if those skilled in the art would supply them. The description must show the invention is new in fact. Excessive detail is not fatal unless fraudulent or rendering essentials obscure. If skilled persons can practise the invention from the description (perhaps using their own ordinary knowledge), the completeness requirement is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A description is intelligible when the language and the methods of statement convey to the reader the exact ideas embodied in the subject or act described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligibility demands phraseology and sentence arrangement that make statements clear and plain to skilled artisans. Unintelligible patents (too brief, overly prolix, using strange words, or confused arrangement) are void. An inventor's or attorney's personal understanding is not proof of intelligibility; the specification must be intelligible to the ordinary skilled reader to whom it is addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification language must be 'full, clear, concise, and exact' / reasonable certainty in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory standard: the Description must be in terms 'full, clear, concise, and exact.' What is claimed as new should appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims/specification should not leave the scope of the invention to minute inferences or conjecture. The patent must show with reasonable certainty what the patentee claims as new; otherwise the public cannot know the exclusive right. Reasonable certainty is judged against what the specification states and what a person skilled in the art would understand from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency to make and use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description is sufficient if, from it aided by the drawings, model, and other parts of the application taken together, a person skilled in the art could construct and use the invention as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement means the skilled artisan can make and use the invention by following the specification without undue experimentation or requiring inventive skill beyond their ordinary mechanical powers and information. If practicing the invention requires invention or substantial experimentation, the specification is insufficient and the patent may be void. Corrections by other parts of the application (drawings, model) can cure defects in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity is fatal when substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Description fails in correctness, completeness, or intelligibility such that ambiguity exists to any considerable degree, that ambiguity is fatal to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts historically showed some indulgence for honest mistakes, but substantial ambiguity that misleads skilled persons will invalidate the patent. Ambiguity can be fatal irrespective of the inventor's intent. Distinctions are drawn between mere defective/ambiguous disclosure (which may void the patent) and deliberate concealment (which may require proof of fraudulent intent depending on statutory interpretation and cases). The jury may infer fraudulent intent from circumstances when required to decide concealment issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness must fit the subject and skilled audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The definiteness of a specification must vary with the nature of its subject; descriptions are addressed to those skilled in the art and may leave something to their skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The level of specificity required depends on the complexity and nature of the invention; the patentee may rely on the reader's ordinary skill to supply routine details (e.g., exact temperatures, well-known modifications). But the specification must not mislead or give vague/uncertain directions that impair construction or use. Examples: temperature ranges may be described imprecisely when precise points cannot reasonably be stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to describe common or well-known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description need not describe what is in common use; well-known processes and devices need not be described in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of commonplace implements, materials, or methods is acceptable where those skilled in the art would understand their application. Similarly, not all uses of the invention must be recited. However, omission of material parts necessary for practice is not permitted; the balance is whether the skilled reader can use the disclosure to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors in naming or theory tolerated if invention clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes in naming the invention, or in assigning it to its proper class, and erroneous theories as to causes do not render the Description insufficient if the invention itself clearly appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical or theoretical errors, wrong names, and unfounded statements about results are consistent with substantial correctness provided they do not mislead the skilled reader about essential features. Immateral errors are typically overlooked; material omissions or misleading errors are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive prolixity not fatal unless fraudulent or obscuring essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the Description is excessive it is still sufficient, unless the redundancy is fraudulent or renders the essential parts of the Description uncertain and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundancy alone does not defeat the specification; the test is whether the surplus detail either conceals essential matter or creates uncertainty sufficient to mislead a person skilled in the art. Fraudulent padding intended to mislead can render a patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of minor details or alternative embodiments not fatal if skilled person can practice invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description need not mention all things that may be used if those which are named will answer the purpose; omissions of appliances, modifications, or processes which skilled persons would know are often acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee need not enumerate every possible implementation or minor detail so long as the specification puts before a person skilled in the art an accurate and entire picture sufficient to enable construction and use. The omission becomes problematic only if it prevents the skilled person from practicing the invention or conceals material parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be read in context and interpreted for skilled reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of the specification is to be considered in connection with its context: clauses together, drawings, model, petition, oath, and other application parts; read as if the invention were present and the reader skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should give effect to the specification as a whole and give the skilled reader the modifications and understandings that such a reader would supply. Claims and descriptions are to be construed in light of accompanying materials and the perspective of the ordinary artisan, not by isolated literalism or by the patentee's private understanding.
